August 11, 1980
Conducted by Bill Kirchner

S. & S. REPORTING CO., INC.

MR. KIRCHNER: Today is August 11, 1980 and we're sitting in the home of Eddie Sauter in West Nyack, New York, and my name is Bill Kirschner.
Eddie, just for the sake of convenience, why don't we go chronologically; that's probably the easiest way to catch everything.
On two or three different sources it's stated that you were born on December 2, 1914 in Brooklyn; is that correct?
That's right.
Okay; let's start from there.
Did you have a musical family?
Not really.

Early on though I do remember there was a family, a very famous painter who had a farm up on Congers, Andrew Davies, and the kids used to walk to Nyack from their farm. They still have a very good farm.
They were possessors of a set of bells and they used to ring them, and it fascinated me and I can remember sitting alongside the road, 9W, and it was not a national highway at the time--
This was in Nyack?
Yes.
I'd ring those bells with these kids. I couldn't have been more than four or five years old.

Then musically after that, I think it was the normal thing in high school and church--grammar school even--when I was nine years old, the family went to Europe; my father was German and we went to visit his family.

We went on an English ship, the Olympic, as I recall in 1924. I remember being enchanted with the orchestra playing on the ship, and that lead to my getting a trumpet. I'm sure there must have been something before that but I really don't know

what it could have been.
I got a trumpet in Bremen,
Germany. I started with a flugal horn, actu-
ally. It was in the key of F; no, it was not
rotary.

That started me with lessons,
I was playing drums at the same time; there
was an organ around the house that my father
played. There was a phonograph with records
of Caruso--who else at that time--pretty
awful stuff.

The radio was just coming out
and I disobeyed all laws and stayed up until
the wee hours in grammar school, listening.
Ellington used to be on all the time. My
favorite of mine was Hal Kemp in those days.

Do you remember Hal Kemp from
North Carolina?

I've heard the
records, yeah.

In the beginning
it was a dixieland band.
Oh, really?
Yeah. It became society later; it was very collegiate.
I remember my brother taking me to see Tea for Two--No, No, Nanette.
With Ruby Keeler.
Was Ruby Keeler in that?
Was she in the oririnal or was she in the revival a few years ago.
She was?
Yeah, she was the headliner of the revival.
She's still around; no kidding.
No, I don't think it was Ruby Keeler; it was someone else.
That was like 1925?
Something like that.
I remember going to the Mangrove Grill at that time to hear Hal Kemp. We used to go to the Chinese restaurant for lunch and they'd always have a band playing. Sometimes they were pretty good.

I used to go to Brooklyn to sit in, at nightclubs, when I was a kid; I used to take the railroad, sleep all night in the Erie Railroad station in Hoboken, get the morning train back home and go to school the next day.
You were a pretty precocious kid.
I guess so, looking back at it.

At that time I guess it must have been late grammar school and I began taking trumpet lessons at Teacher's College by a guy named Harvey Sartorius who became a music teacher on Long Island somewhere. Somebody must remember him, Harvey was quite a guy. He introduced me to a lot of these
people so that I could sit in. That was all trumpet.
Did you have any brothers or sisters who played?

I have a brother who was really an electrical engineer in Bell Labs and music was his hobby. He did one of the varsity shows at Stevens Tech. He was always dillying around writing and interested in people like Gershwin. He lead me into that too.
In those days around here we had kids bands and that's really what kicked me off, I think; I'd make arrangements for that band.
How old were you then?
I must have been in high school, beginning with the first year already; it had to be that. I had a friend of the family who was a passenger agent, American passenger agent, for the French Line,
and he got us dates every summer for the kids band, going back and forth playing on the French Line, which was quite an experience.
I'm sure.
Of all things, the French Line was the peak of it.
What was it, a ten piece band?
No, three or four or five; we'd go from one end of the ship to the other.
That was the high school period.

Then I went to Columbia after that and a similar thing happened there. I joined the Columbia Blue Lions which was there college jazz band, I guess. They had no music department at Columbia, I couldn't study music there.
What were you studying?
Just general.
Liberal arts?
Liberal arts; yes.
It says in John Chilton's book that you originally played drums.

Yes, with a trumpet band; I played the trumpet and the drums. I used to take dates like that. I had a record player, it even had a straw needle on it and I played the drums with whoever was around on the record or the radio. I played the trumpet at the same time. That all went together.
That must have made you more marketable as a player.

I don't know; in those days I didn't think of it in those terms. It was curiosity. There were all sorts of instruments that I would rent from the high school, tenor saxophone, tuba; things like that. I was always fascinated by the sound of the instruments, any kind of instrument. I even tried the fiddle but that didn't
But as far as the violin goes, you learned the mechanics of the instrument.
Or the Ukelele, they're about the same thing; you knew that you had to move your fingers this way.
At least you know what works and doesn't work for a string player.
No, no.
Really?
Shall we digress and get into that or shall we continue where we are?
It might help to stick to where we are for the time being. We'll have to make sure you get into that. One thing before we go any further, what were your parents' names?
My mother's name was Julia Groeter, it was Swiss; and my
father's name was August Sauter; he was German.
What did they do for a living?

My father was a florist, he had greenhouses in Nyack. I guess before that he came to this country as a landscape gardener. He had done that in France, in England and in Switzerland. This goes back into the nineteenth century.
Were they both born in Europe?
No, my mother was born in Manhattan, of Swiss parentage.
When did your father come here?
1890; something like that. It must have been because they were well established by the time of the Gold Rush of 1898.
Well let's see;
we've gotten as far as the Columbia Blue Lions.
Let me think. In 1930--this is two years before I went to Columbia--
When did you go to Columbia?
'32. Archie Bleyer was--
"Mr. Stock Arranger."

Yes; he also had a correspondence course and I took that and got to know him. In '31--I think it was '31, he started a band and I got to play in it, this was over in Westchester somewhere. Fletcher Henderson at that time had gone down the street--there were bands all over the Post Road in those days. I got to know Fletcher later in Benny's band. It kind of convinced me I was never a very good trumpet player. I had gotten kicked in the lip when
I was playing football in high school before that. I played a great low G. I did that in Red Norvo's band, still playing trumpet then.
And mellophone too?
Yeah, that was earlier; that was a freak.

1930, Archie Bleyer, I was still in college when Archie got a job at the Enpire Ballroom--Empire. There's a ballroom on 53rd and Broadway, it's no longer there. They used to have elevated tracks there. What was the name of it? It really doesn't make any difference.
Wait a minute, that had to be even later. I was in college then, so that period with Archie Bleyer must have gone on some time.
According to Chilton's, you said work with Archie Bleyer in 1932.
That's probably true; '31 also.

Then came Columbia and I went back to Archie with the band. '33 it must have been as well, and it must have been in '33 in that ballroom. I used to trudge up all the way to 53rd Street with the trumpet case at three in the morning, alone, nobody was around.
That was before the IRT?
No, the IRT was very much there, I just did it.
Why?
I liked to, I guess.
I wouldn't do it today.
No, I wouldn't recommend it, especially with a horn.
We used to do it, and also all through the thirties we used to wander around through Harlem and nobody ever

did anything.

I don't know if it was because of our youth or there was a different attitude in those days. Harlem was quite a tourist attraction then.

We'll go up to 1934 and '35, I had played summers with the kid band I was telling you about.
One question about that, it says in Chilton's book that you travelled extensively throughout Europe.
Yes.
That's when you were doing the French Line?
Yes.
Where did you go?
Switzerland, France, Germany, England; that was it. We didn't get down into Italy. We had to do it between trips.
Did you see or hear anything notable?

Only collecting an ambiance, certainly a feeling and I get that feeling every time I listen to Stravinsky of that period or Ravel in that period. It doesn't take too much imagination to go back a few years and catch Debussy either. It had a different feeling than it does today. New York had a different feeling. How do you describe that? I don't know. Europe was always a difficult place, I'm sure it was, but it also had more peripheral dimensions than it does now. It was impersonal, but not so impersonal. There were regionalisms; France was very definitely French. You don't any longer feel that. Britain was an island and there were walls around that island. When you entered the place you felt you were entering a medieval castle.
You almost think of Europe as an entity anymore.
They were locked in, local, regional cultures. And that's what gave them their tastes, their flavor. It was true in this country too.
Around that time I guess you were with Charlie Barnett; right?

I was getting into that and that's where I met Red Norvo. But before that--remember we were talking about Cozy Cole, with the kids band I was in; at the same time I was in Columbia Blue Lions, ran them both--I didn't run Columbia but the other one I was involved in. We got a job at the--this was the Empire Ballroom, and Benny Carter and the other band--we were the relief band--
That was like '33 wasn't it?

We also played with that band Ben Martin's Riviera at the Jersey shore. In that band was Tootie Camarata, who became, I guess, a famous pops conductor later on. And Chris Griffin who was a trumpet player at CBS for many, many years; Joe Moody. He wasn't directly involved in that one but it all came about from getting to know Joe in that period; he had his own group.

Tootie got a job with Charlie Barnet and got me in there and at that point I left Columbia. I had begun to take lessons-- the first lessons were with Archie Bleyer, and there was a guy named Billie Fisher--there was a Scott Fisher too at that time--I don't know if it does anything to you. They had a band, a North Jersey band, Billie was a precocious sort of saxophone player and arranger. He became an arranger for CBS for many, many years; he had gotten very commercial. I'm trying to remember the connection.
Anyway, somehow all through

this, Tootie got involved and Tootie was interested in writing, as I was. Tootie used to take down dictation from Joe Moore/ who was blind. Joe on the piano would tell him what notes to put where and who to give it to. He'd hear all this and Tootie learned to write this way.

At one point we decided we were going to take some lessons and we both went to an old style--I wouldn't call him a martinette, but a very rigid instrucoor type that Billie Fisher had and his name was (inaudible). That began the whole thing of studying. Tootie did it too.

Later on we both went to Teacher's College. At that point Tootie went off with Jimmy Dorsey and started to make a big name for himself. I stuck there, I went with Benny but I didn't make a big name for myself. That was after and we're jumping the gun here.
I'd hate to have to listen to
Why don't we go back to Charlie Barnet.
That was important because that's where I met Red and Mildred, (phonetic spelling). Red was always running away from Mildred; I guess it had a tendency to be sparkling, that marriage.
Yes; I've heard.
Red took to playing piano in Barnet's band.
What kind of a piano player was he?
He's good. Not forceful, but he played piano like he played (inaudible). He was a writer too, by the way. He wrote some pieces that were excellent, "Dance of the Octopus".
And he did the transcription of "In A Mist".
Yes.
Those are great records.
They sure are.
He did the charts for those, for "Dance of the Octopus"; he did the scoring for that, with the bass clarinet?
I think he did. He wrote the piece "Octopus".
Right.
And I think that he probably did that too. He confesses to not having enough patience to do it.

I began, at that time, as (Cyrinus) Tootie did, for Barnet and I guess Mildred and Red sort of liked it and Mildred asked me to do something for her and that's how they kicked the whole thing off on me, because I never really thought of being a professional writer. I hadn't thought of being a professional anything at that point.
I was making money to go back to college. Meanwhile, I didn't know what for either. I liked to play and it had been my complete life, as you can tell, from the beginning.
I needed instruction and I was well aware of that. I wanted something more than I was getting from sheer experience. It wasn't enough and it's never been. Don't let me wander.
It's okay, it all fits in.
That must have been '34. Barnet's band went to New Orleans and got tangled up with Huey Long. Huey Long hated the band.
Why?
He didn't like it.
Did someone do something to antagonize him?
Maybe it played too loud. Something of that nature.
Anyway, we were out from one
night to the next and we came wandering back to New York. Charlie, of course, had flew out, he didn't care.
He had plenty of money.
He had plenty of money; he left us to our own devices.
There was a guitar player from Atlanta, Buff--I can't recall his name. A wife, little baby.
Buff Estes?
That's a saxophone player.

There were no interstates in those days, there were mud roads, and it rained. I remember going through Alabama and Mississippi and getting stuck in mud; no money, so we didn't sleep, I don't know what we ate.
I recall arriving at Washington and we stayed in a flop house, which you could do. This is in the middle of the Depression.
It wasn't that bad, but it was a flop house and everytime I go back I wonder where it was. I have no idea where it could have been.
It's probably long torn down.
It was one of those corner places.
Was Red with you at the time?
No, Red made up with Mildred.
The two of you were roommates for a while, weren't you? When he was on the outs with Mildred?

Yes. One time--this may have been before that even, when we were playing the Apollo and I didn't want to commute, I stayed at the Teresa, and there I do recall getting some strange looks, because people just didn't do that. I was very naive and I didn't know anything about that. I had no sense of

anything of that nature.
Then Red got tangled up with
Mildred and then came to stay there a couple
of nights and then up in Maine, having been
in New Orleans, there was a Rudy Vallee band
and they got stranded in Maine too.

Red went up on that, Mildred
came up and before Mildred came, Red roomed
with me too, always encouraging me to write.
I tried writing for that band; Tootie wrote
for the band too.

I guess it was before that I
had done the first thing for Mildred in the
theatre in New Jersey, where Barnet had some-
how got up with Mildred, through Red, I guess.

After that Red started this
small group with Dave Barbour and Stuie
Pletcher and Herbie Haymer, Pete Peterson.
And no drums?

Yes, Maurice
Purtill.
There was a while
when there was no drums; correct? It was kind of famous for that reason, as I recall.
It might have been. I always remember Maurice being there.
Yes; the first one had drums. Let's see, here's January '36 [Stew Fletcher] with Stew Fletcher, Donald McCork, Herbie Haymer, you, Dave Barbour, Pete Peterson, Bob White on drums, and Red.
Bob White came later.
'36; that's a recording.
That could be.
That's when you did "Polly Wolly Doodle".
Yes.
And "Gramercy Square".
I don't know why I wrote myself in on the mellophone; that's probably what it was.
Was mellophone
Because of the bad lip, you mean?
Yes.
It did, and also it didn't require one to be as precise in intonation I guess. You really didn't have to be a good player.

Stu was wonderful. In an interview once we were talking about Stu, they asked me about him, I said Stu was never very good, but that is not the case. He was not an accomplished trumpet player, but as a jazz musician he was superb, and I didn't make that clear, and I would like to make that clear now.
I know if he ever heard that interview it must have hurt him. It was not done maliciously.
Michael Brooks talked to you when they did the Red Norvo reissue, at Columbia Special Products; right?
Yes.
I didn't get that impression.
You didn't?
I got the impression from what you said that he just wasn't a very good--an extremely polished musician, but he was a talented jazz trumpet player.
If you got that, that was fine, because I learned--I think I learned more jazz from Stuie because he would always try for things and miss, but it was his recouping that made the thing--
Miles Davis has made a career out of that.
That's right, and so have I.
To me most of the fun is reaching for something, not quite knowing where you're going and if you miss, use it, and I learned that from Stu and I think that's an artistic precept.
No, I didn't get that impression at all.
Okay.
But you did most of the writing them for Red's group, then?
Right.
They were playing at the Hickory House for a while?
Right.

Then they wandered around 52nd Street and then he wanted to do a bigger band and we went up to Syracuse, I think, and then we went to the west coast after that. I think it was (inaudible), in Los Angeles.

I played trumpet until that summer of '37 and then gave it up. I met my wife at this period, she came from northern Wisconsin. I went up there for a mastoid operation and she was a nurse in those days,
she helped take care of me. That's how I met her.
We're an old fashioned marriage.
We're looking at a copy of the New Yorker with a picture of a distinguished three story house and there's a sign in front that says, The Smythes. Since 1937, an old fashioned marriage.
Pretty shortly after that, Red started his big band; right?
That was his big band already.
Oh, okay, that was '36?
Yes. That was the Chicago.
I think the Commodore Hotel in New York was the first job; they went to Boston, Syracuse. All the time I was playing trumpet until the Black Hawk, and writing.
When did he decide to make the jump into having a big band?
He must have been considering it, but I'm sure it happened--
(Side A of Tape 1 ended at this point. Transcript will continue with Side B.)
(Side B of Tape 1 begins at this point.)
--that last winter, '35 and '36. That's when Benny had started to hit it. Who else? I guess the Dorsey Brothers. Bob Crosby too. Artie Shaw.

It's interesting, I was at the Institute of Jazz Studies last Friday playing somethings that you had written that I hadn't heard, and I heard some of those things from the Red Norvo period like "Love Song to a Chambermaid".
That was in '36.
And things that were a little later, like "Remember".
That wasn't later, really.
It was recorded in '37.
'36-'37. It started--the first job was

in June, because I had made arrangements before that, to get ready for that. "Remember" I think was already in the works in the autumn of '36, and recorded in '37; that's true. I remember it well, in Chicago in the Padded Cell.
What was the Padded Cell?
It was a studio, near the water tower, but it was all thick padding. There was no reverberation of any sort. That's the way they did it in those days. That's why it sounds that way.
The way that band was, it was probably just about perfect because it was a very light, kind of ethereal band.
They were all recorded in that fashion in those days, and I think that is one of the reasons they sound that way. I don't think they materially sounded different from the way a band sounds
now, without amplification. There was no-- this padding took up all the tempo of the instruments, they don't sing. People think that's the way they played; it isn't so, it was a recording technique.

I can remember some of the most thrilling experiences I had is walking into a room and hearing a live band being part of the room, because amplification was not part of the scene in those days. They had one mike maybe for announcement and that's all. It didn't do anything to amplify the band.
So what you heard was coming from the group and the room itself and it left me with memories of sound that I don't get any longer.
How could you get sounds like low register clarinet and bass clarinet across, say in a live situation, without amplification?
I don't think they went in so much for huge auditoriums, where

you got millions of people; they didn't do that. If you did--they had some in Madison Square, but I think already they were using amplification of an awful sort. It didn't mean very much, but mostly I think they were smaller rooms, nightclubs.

Sometimes other people would play soft too, and in those days Benny got kicked out of an east side hotel he was playing for playing too loud. People wanted to talk, so the emphasis was on playing softly, and we really did play soft whether you did it on a clarinet or a saxophone didn't make very much difference. It was more difficult to play soft on a trumpet.
That was any specialty of Red's. They used to call us the subtle swing.
It was a marvelous band.
Sure; but it was very soft. I've always been attracted to that, we used to try to have dynamics in
soft and some of the most exciting things were very very soft, like a whisper sometimes, to come down from something loud into that.

It struck me when I heard the things that you did for Red, you're familiar with Gerry Mulligan's concert bands of the early sitties, and it struck me how much the charts that Mulligan and Bob Brookmeyer and Gary McFarland did twenty five years later, how much they sounded like what you had done in the late thirties.

It is the same very light, very woodwindish sort of colorations, a lot of clarinet lead in the reed section, but using the clarinet and the lower and middle registers. There's a lot of similarity, I was surprised by that.
I hadn't thought of that. You're probably right.
Very similar instrumentation too.
What did he have?
Mulligan had three trumpets, three trombones, four saxes and himself playing and then bass and drums and later he had guitar.
Did he have a piano?
He played it once in a while. There was "a" piano player. He would play it once in a while or Brookmeyer would.
Good choice. Brookmeyer is one of my favorites.
Oh, he's marvelous.
I remember that band. I did something I had done for Ray McKenley and reworked it.
Which one was that?
I forgot the title; it was one of those that Ray never played.
I took it to Germany with me; there were four of them and I think there are still two I haven't heard.
One of them I did for Gerry and it was not his style either; he didn't want to do it. He put it away and that was it.
Oh, that's a shame.
Where were we?
We were talking about Norvo's band.
Do you want to talk about some of the players on the band?
Herbie Haymer?
Yes.
Too bad he died so young. That was really silly. Red tells me he was hit by a car coming out of a recording studio, crossing a street. Some dame was drunk.
Pete Peterson; he's gone now.
Moe Purtill was on that for a while, as you mentioned.
Yes.
Dave Barbour. And the clarinet player was who? Cook McKirk, Cook Don McKirk.
Later on it was Slats Long.
Yes.
I'm looking at a book by John Chilton called Who's Who of Jazz. Herbie Haymer was killed in a car crash while driving home--
He wasn't driving, Red said.
Really?
He was walking across the street, coming out of the recording studio. Red told me that. I always thought it was driving too.
That's interesting. Chilton claims he was killed in a car
crash while driving home from a Frank Sinatra recording session.
The Frank Sinatra recording session is probably correct. You can verify it with Red. Red is the one who informed me he was not driving, he was walking across the street.
I always thought he had gotten loaded and was driving, but the woman who was driving was loaded.
That sounds like some of the stories I heard of people living out in Malibu and getting drunk.
After Slats Long there was Hank D'Amico?
Yes, we got him in Albany. He joined us in Syracuse; he was marvelous. Drank too much, killed him eventually.
Louis Mucci came with us then; then Al Mastren, Carmen's brother, who runs a restaurant in Cohoes now, I think. I have
Bill Miller.
Bill Miller, yes. Who else?
Jerry Jerome was on there for a while; wasn't he?
Yes, he was. I just don't recall the period he was.
There's a recording for September of '37.
Yes, he was.
"Russian Lullaby," "Clap Hands", "Here Comes Charlie."
That's from on the west coast.
In Hollywood; that's right.
Jerry Jerome was there; I'll be darned. Is Lenny Goldstein in that?
Yes, playing alto.
Lenny Goldstein is the father of a famous rock star these days. What does he call himself; Rupert Holmes. Do you know him?
I've heard of him; yes.
Everybody else has, everybody seems to know him so he must be quite famous. Who was the trumpet player in that band?
George Wettling was there for a while.
Yes, that was in New York.
George Berg.
Yes.
He didvery well in the studios.
Jerry Jerome as well. He was a commercial entrepreneur-- commercials entrepreneur.
When Red did his oral history interview, he told one story that I'll have to tell you because it concerns you.
Red said that one day that for some reason Mildred had done something that annoyed you--
I know what you're going to say.
--so you wrote a really hard modulation in one of the charts and she just went through it flawlessly.
That's right.
Do you remember which chart that was?
There were a couple of them.
This was more than a one time occurrence?
That's true. I think "Smoke Dreams" might have been one of them, but that was a little
early on, and another one was a Gershwin tune. I remember the incident; but she didn't miss a beat piece.
Let's talk about her and Red a little more. What kind of relationship did you have with her?
Oh, wonderful. They were like big brother and big sister or mother or father; however you want to look at it. What an environment for a young person to be exposed to, because--
You were only about twenty four, twenty five years old.

No, I was younger than that, I was only about twenty when I first went. Everywhere else had been commercialism, and here was always--the first thing was concern for the music. It was always that way and no where else did I encounter that and I always look back and I think that is one of the reasons why I have
not been commercially successful. I'm frightened of boredom, I don't ever want to become bored with what I'm doing, and so far, I've been lucky, I haven't.

I think it comes from them, the same attitude stays with me and a thing like that has to be implanted when you're young or it won't work. I don't know if it's part of personality or the result of having someone to show you something that you know is the ultimate truth. If you find it early on-- I suppose you can discover it later--but it gets involved with a set of values.

I think it's very important; it's given me a love for music that I never lost, and I don't want to lose it. I can go just so far, I can always give; I can bend, I'm forced to bend if I want to make a living, we all have to do that, but I don't want to lose that and I don't think anyone can get it away from me anymore. I know they've tried very hard. I've been caspigated endlessly
for having that attitude. There is such a huge respect for cynicism in the commercial world, and I'm accused of being cynical. I don't get that at all.
In any case, you were in the right place at the right time.
For that, yes.
I have always felt very close to them, always liked them, always happy to see them.
Mildred passed away a good thirty years ago. While she was here, it was always the same thing, it was always at the request of someone. She was a real artist, and Red is too.
Do you know Mildred's story of Bing Crosby?
And her brother?
Yes.
Do you mean how she got on the Whitman Band?
Yes.
I've heard it, yes.
Her brother was one of the Rhythm Boys.
Yes, but I think she got him the job and in turn he got her the job. It was pretty weird.
(Inaudible)
I'm glad I have it, it's a 1944 radio program with Mildred and Red on it and it's one of the only times I've heard Mildred recording where she sounds like Mildred.
She didn't record the way she really sang?
Did you ever hear a Basie record of that period that sounded like Basie? Not really; they always did something somewhere.
It's hard for me to tell, because the only time I've heard Basie live is in the sixties and seventies
when his style was altogether different.

Well it was a roaring band. I heard them first in the Grand Terrace in Chicago and it always had that same thing, but never on a record. It had to do with putting limiters on the top and bottom, I guess.
Well with the dynamic range, sure.
The rhythm section was never placed right, it was either off or it was too close, or one thing or another. It never sounded right.
Well, Mildred had that thing too. She was never as loose on a record as she was on this '44 record.
I remember in rooms how she would sound and in Novello's band, it was never recorded either. It had a much different thing about it than records showed.
It was like before when I spoke about walking into a room and hearing a band.
It was a brighter band in person you mean?
Yeah, and it had more--I would say style.

In maybe a more impersonal fashion, do you mean?

All right.

volved in the early sixties, and when the
phone rings, it's usually a Broadway show.
I don't turn them down, I'm

If you have any desire to make

You mentioned that the other day.

I heard A Little Night Music was that way too. I think you have to give Sondheim his due, and I never know how much goes to the orchestrator and how much goes to composer. It depends really on the guy who does--I use that word advisedly, because most Broadway writers are not composers; they're tunesmiths. There is a huge difference. But Sondheim, not having worked with him, I really don't know. I have a suspicion that he watches his notes carefully.

I worked with people like that; Robert Emmet Dolling was one, and he translated his setting, he made his--even their orchestral settings--we were talking about this sort of thing before, about Hollywood,

It's hard to tell on a Broadway musical in any case, if it comes out being a unified affair, someone had to make sure that it did that and that person has to have power. It can be the producer, it can be the director or the guy that wrote the tunes, but certainly never the orchestrator; he doesn't have that kind of power. He's the low man on the totem pole.

There's only one person lower than an orchestrator in a Broadway musical, and that's they guys who play in the band, the pit. The whole essence of a Broadway musical, to me, is a combination of soap opera and vaudeville, and in both cases
Music is being used as a secondary function.
Always, in show business.

Very little, no. That was not a concern of mine in those days. My main concern was leaving Red. I truly didn't want to do that and something told me to do it.

It was shocking to walk in, because I never expected anything like that.
Red Norvo wasn't a teen idol.
He hadn't become that.
Red made a lot of fads at the right time, but at the same period I was leaving Red, Glenn Miller had just begun (inaudible), so he walked off with it that year.
I think it was a year later I went to the Ben Franklin in Philadelphia with Red and he followed Harry James or
Harry James followed Red, I forgot now. Harry James took off and left Red there, because Red was always too good. That was always his problem, he liked music.
Harry was a good looking guy and a good player (inaudible).
It might have been Red's instrument; I doubt it though. At that time he was still playing xylophone, maybe tha's what caused him to switch to vibraphone; I don't know. But Red's still there.
Yeah, and still playing beautifully.

You bet he is. I wonder if he regrets it; I really don't know. I know that shortly after that he gave up all ideas of having a band of his own, and a big one. He went to work for Woody, he spent a couple of years on the beach.
He had some marvelous small groups, the trio he had with
Tal Farlow.
Wasn't that something?
Beautiful.

Yeah, that was early fifties.
That was a wonderful group. Tal Farlow was another story. I see in the paper he just came to New York again.

That's Bill's hometown, you know.
Really? I didn't know that.
Basie too is from Red Bank; that's right there.
Anyway, so you
Yes. I had to do two or three a week.

Yes; and that was nice. Because of that I could now take lessons, which is what I wanted to do. There was always something beckoning, something beyond which I had. I still do that. That's part of the Judeo-Christian heritage. That's the way it is; I still keep looking for something that's not there, or that isn't immediately apparent and I felt illiterate, I didn't like the feeling and I wanted to do something about it, so I went to these various people.
Were you able to incorporate any of the things you learned
in charts and various things you did for Benny?

One doesn't learn that. It's a process of absorption and the way you think, and what I learned I really don't know. I couldn't enumerate it today, I wouldn't begin to tell you what I knew. I don't teach because I don't feel secure I think people want to know specifics and I don't know that I'm prepared. I can't give specifics to someone else without drawing up, which you have seen me do too often here; if they want something else, I don't know. I think the function of a teacher, the way I see it is, to inspire somehow someone to seek his own path and his own levels, whatever that may be.
I think you're absolutely right.
Techniques are too often self serving, they certainly have time
limits on them. They work for a given period and not much more.
You can look for general principles, and I think they are there; I keep looking and I'm not so sure that I ever do find any though.

If there is anything such as a general principle, it's more osmosis and too diffuse to verbalize. The moment you verbalize it, to begin isolating certain segments of it that are convenient, and you're allowing to escape probably the most important part of what was happening.

A lot of people call it improvising, but it's not necessarily so. I think that probably is the enticement behind the contact of improvising, but that alone to me is not enough. It almost requires constant repetition in order to achieve, occasionally, something that you haven't done before. You have to do mostly what you have been doing. It's not as free as critics
have us believe.
There are too many people who think they're improvisors who to me are pattern players. They're not really improvising, they're giving back to you what they've--
Whatever is their habit. It becomes a habit.
A talent, a real talent, will always still do this. Ninety percent of what a real talent does is habit, but his habits then may be more perceptive.

Occasionally also, if he has allowed himself to develop in that way, will do something that he is not aware that he has done until after he has done it, and then it becomes part of his habit. But that's for him; he's found that and he really can't do that to anyone else.
I've always been leery of methods, and yet you have to have something, when you're beginning particularly, something

to latch onto. But I've seen so many people get on the thing and it's false and they re- tain this falseness all their lives, or they spend an inordinate amount of effort to try to get rid of it, without really knowing what they're trying to get in its place. That's the responsibility of a teacher that overwhelms me.
That didn't have much to do with Benny; did it?
Who cares? It has to do with you and that's what we're talking about.

I'd like to talk for a few minutes about I guess what I consider and what a lot of other people consider, the most important things you did for Benny, things like 'Benny Rides Again' and 'Clarinet a la King' and 'Superman' and works like that. What do you think about those?
I really don't know. When I listen to those things, for me

it's like picking up a photograph, it brings back--it's always a nostalgic enterprise for me--it brings back smells, much better than a photograph. It's a whole sense of what it is like to be around then. That's how I see it, I don't see it in any other terms.
So that doesn't help you very much.
Did you feel that you were doing something particularly ambitious when you were writing those, because they sound very ambitious?

No, I think that whenever I've done anything it's what I could do at that moment. I don't like to pander, because I feel that everytime you do something--I like to do something that stretches, that pushes the limit, because if you don't, you fall back into that sort of pattern that we were discussing before. Ambitious is not the term I would use; it's what I could do and what
concerned me most of the time was that sort of thi g. I did it in the form it was, because that's who I was doing it for. If there was another situation it wouldn't have been that at all.
One thing that was a big factor, I'm sure, was that you were writing pieces that had to fit on one side of a 78.

Yes, everything you did had to have a limit and more than that, disc jockeys wouldn't play it unless it was two fifty--they wanted it less than three minutes or else it interfered with the commercials. Also in those days jukeboxes were a big thing and they wanted to make it for the jukebox.
I'm sure it was especially crucial in the case of those pieces, because you weren't just taking a pop tune and writing two to three choruses
In those days--
In other words, did you feel restricted in any way or hampered in the way you wrote those because they had to be a specific length?

No. I think if you begin to do too much of them you begin to think that way. If you write too many commercials you begin to think in terms of thirty seconds of the minute, but barring that, you can write a concise piece of music in three minutes, and sometimes better than if you take thirty to forty. I've heard a lot of thirty and forty minute pieces that shouldn't be that at all. They should stop abruptly at three minutes.
I think what was different there was the type of form. It was sort of an open ended thing where it closed at the end. I'm sure I was overwhelmed by Ellington's band at

that time, they way they got through their things; but I couldn't do that because I wasn't there. If I had been part of Ellington's band maybe, but those things are hung together in such a way. So having them hang together got to be very important and I guess the only way I could do it at that time was that way. Today it might be a little different, but it worked.
Frankly, I think it's--just to take an arbitrary example, "Superman" is just a good a piece and as ambitious a piece as "A Concerto for Cootie" that Duke wrote for Cootie, and works just as well.

Whether it's as valuable as a piece of art I don't know. Duke's certainly was; whether mine was, I don't know. It wasn't done for that reason, it was done just to do it. It worked out to be fine, but that piece is a little longer.
It's about four
It was an LP; no, it wasn't an LP; what was it? Four and a half minutes.
A twelve inch 78.
It's sort of an scope or something where you try to make the whole thing hang together.
I think they all certainly did.
They did, for whatever it was; they did.
What was the band's reaction?
I don't know, they didn't quite cotton to it. They wanted something else.
In those days--and I think you still get that--where they want pretty much what's familiar, they don't like anything that goes off a little way.
Benny didn't play this stuff for a long time because he used to complain they were too classical. He made records of them but after that, no.
They weren't the thing he would put on gigs very often?
No.

I read some comment by Jerry Jerome to the effect that apparently the band, they sounded like they played them very well, but apparently they felt that they really had to scuffle and be on their toes to play them.
That's right, they had to use a different mental set for these things, and these others were more comfortable. I've heard that.
You weren't writing thirty two bar choruses.
It was more compositional and that I guess was my thing, that's why I became what I was, otherwise I
would have been a player.
Do you have a favorite of all those pieces?
Not really; no. Again, the time evokes for me, I was young.

One thing I thought was interesting was when you had Sauter-Finegan, when you did the one album, Memories of Goodman and Miller, where you each rescored some of the things you had written during that period--
I changed very little.
I noticed that.
I didn't think that would be honest, I couldn't really see the purpose of that.
If anything it was like you had more orchestral to play with, so it was like seeing a movie in technicolor that you formerly had seen in black
and white. The form was basically the same.

It was all the same thing except reorchestrated. I could see no reason to change it because if I were to change it, why do that piece. So that's why it was that way. Also, it would be a lie to the title of the album.
I did that while I was in Germany, by the way. That came in by mail.
Then as it right after the band disbanded?

A couple of years; we disbanded--the government was threatening to take all the money at the gate to pay the taxes we owed them, and that would have left us stranded who knows where, and we were constantly being sent out on the road, at a loss. We never made any money with that thing, not enough to keep the thing going.
Toward the end of it, they were being to have State Department tours and we thought that that would be just a great thing
for publicity.
Yeah, Dizzy's band did one and Woody's band.
We got the message that they thought we were not representatively American. They didn't want to send us abroad. Another person said--
Who is the idiot who made that decision?
Some critic, a very famous one, who was on the board.
Who was it?

I don't want to say. But it was also suggested that maybe it was too expensive, because we didn't have a huge percussion section, but I don't see how that could have been. They could send a lot of percussion too.
They could send symphony orchestras abroad.
So I have a sneaky suspicion it was knocked out by the critics.

Anyway, we decided to stop it for a while and tell our agents not until you can book us in such a way that we can come out at least being even, and that was the end of the band. It never went out again.
That's a shame.
It was.
Unless you could grab and somehow influence the thinking of the time, it was wrong, because right after that, rock shot up.

You've been telling me about the life of jazz in New York; I was not aware of it. More had been going on, because I thought it was nothing; you never hear of it. I don't know why, but I have never really been that involved with jazz. That's not right either. Something's wrong. Why? I don't know.
I don't know if it's a question of right or wrong. From my own standpoint, if you get involved in the

New York scene as far as Jazz goes, you make it a point to know what's happening just because you're part of that, but from what I've been able to observe in various people who I respect, it's very easy to get away from that, if you're not really immersed in it.

You can only be immersed in it if you're working in it and that didn't happen. And then for publicity and even in clubs, when you read the reviews in the New York Times, it's never that. It's occasionally Zoot and Al or Stan at a club somewhere.
Yeah, you read about established people, you don't read about up and coming people that much, except somebody who becomes the darling of the critics or something like that.
Let's see, let's get back to Benny again.
Don't feel intimidated about
going back and forth, because I think these things all serve a purpose in an interesting way.

--you more or less, I'm on salary, so I have to write two or three of these a week.

I try never to do something that I can't get myself involved in, but sometimes that's not always possible and you have a deadline and you do it. I'm sure that a lot of it was that way. After a while though it got so that I couldn't hear one note going to another, it was too repetitive, too much of the same thing. I just had to stop it. That was panic for a couple of years.
What kind of a relationship did you have with Benny?
A very good one. I always got along with Benny. He had his quirks but you accept those things, everyone does.
In one way or another.
He might have been parsimonious, sometimes thoughtless, but I can accept that.
What about some of the other people on the band? You mentioned--
Jimmy Maxwell?
That's a good start; yeah.
Jimmy, in those days, I considered a good friend of mine. He married a girl who was the sister of Benny's bass player at the time.
Artie Bernstein?

Artie Bernstein. He came to Benny's band from Sacramento. I guess he'd been in Gil Evans' band. I think that's who it was before that. Gil used to have a band in (inaudible) Beach, I remember going down there with Red Norvo
in '38 when he had one there.
What did it sound like? Is that a dumb question?
That's not a dumb question, but I don't know that I can answer it. It was good.
Did it sound like anything that, for example, he wrote later for Claude Barnhill (phonetic spelling), or I won't try to go beyond that?
I can't answer that, I don't know.

But Jimmy, when he came with Benny, was very taken with eastern cultures He used to sleep on a straw mat, lived on bananas and studied Japanes; he used to talk Japanese. This was in 1940, just before the war. He was always a unique human being and turned out to be a very good trumpet player.
Still is.
I know.
He's still a good lead player too. He's gotten more chances I think in recent years to be a soloist, a great plunger player.
Good musician.
No question.

Teddy Wilson; wonderful, a lovely human being. And Fletcher, a very kind human being. Fletcher's wife I used to--Fletcher's wife used to copy from Benny and I'd run things down there at three thirty, four o'clock in the morning and never a problem.
She lived on 138th Street and Lenox Avenue somewhere. Don't go there alone now, especially if you're white. But in those days they didn't do anything.
Horace Henderson in his oral history interview said that Benny used to call Fletcher in the middle of the night and tell him, will you please do such and such a chart, I need it for a recording
session the next day, or something like that. Did you know about any of that, or did that happen to you?
No. He would say something if I somehow sometimes didn't get the two or three a week in. That happened occasionally, but no, he would always take from that.
Did you know Fletcher very well?

How well? I don't know how to answer. I knew him as one would know a co-worker, a close co-worker, which was pretty good. There was always respect and he was always very kind. He was the elder statesman at that point. Benny had built his band around Fletcher's arrangements and I was suppose to imitate that, I think, but I never really could. Maybe Fletcher respected me because I didn't; I don't know.
I imagine he did. Did you get to hear Fletcher's band in its heyday?
Yes, and it sounded awful. Maybe because I heard them always early in the evening. They were down on the Post Road at a place I was working.
This was late twenties, early thirties?
Yes. It was always rather slipshod, but always very much personality involved. I've forgotten who the players were, but that could easily be found out.
Coleman Hawkins probably. He was there until about '34.

If you came in too early, they had a tendency not to play together. It didn't gel until the evening wore on. Duke had a tendency to be that way too. Benny Carter was another one, that came a little later. We talked about
that the other day.
You mentioned briefly that you played opposite his band; you didn't talk about the band at all.
Wonderful band, and great arrangements that he made. Do you remember the theme song he had, Lonesome Nights; do you know that at all?
I've heard it. He had a reputation for being a much--I don't know if the word is stricter, more disciplined bandleader.
I guess so.
He really would rehearse the band until it was incredibly tight.
It was, and in fact Teddy was playing piano before he went with Benny there. Cozy Cole--who were the others? The trombone player.
J.C. Higgenbottom.

Dicky Wells. Benny used to play trumpet, saxophone, play trumpet--and I was a trumpet player in those days--he used the no-pressure system. He balanced it on the palm of his hand and moved all around without effort at all.
He said Doc Cheetam (phonetic spelling) turned him on to that.
Really? Doc's something else. He's a wonderful player.
And that's the way Doc plays still. He's at a forty five degree angle.
Yeah, he does it well.
I think he was having his seventieth birthday at a club over here two or three years ago, so that makes him seventy three or seventy four now.
Yeah.
Unbelieveable; and he plays so well. Not many people can do that.
Did you ever hear the recordings Benny's band did of Spike Hughes' music around that time, around the early thirties?
Spike Hughes?
He was a British composer.
Benny Goodman or Benny Carter?
Benny Carter.
No, no.

He was a British composer who wrote some stuff that was really interesting, kind of Ellington influenced, and they recorded it in New York with Benny's band and they brought in Coleman Hawkins. They were some marvelous records.
I'd love to hear
I'll get a tape sometime and I'll bring it and play it for you.
Anyway, as far as Mr. Goodman is concerned, we spoke of Fletcher. You knew Charlie Christian pretty well?
Again, as a co-worker.
And you said that you even caught tuberculosis.
You could never be certain where you caught it, but I suspect so, because he was pretty sick when he came with the band.

I remember in 1940 going fishing with Lionel and Irving Goodman and Lionel's wife, my wife and Charlie. I don't fish but I went along, it was fun to ride around the island on a boat, and he was pretty sick then. That was the first time I knew that he had
been. I know later on, that following winter, he had a hemorrhage on a plane.
Mel Powell was in that band and Mel got TB too.
They used to rehearse--didn't we put this on tape before, or were we just talking about it?
We talked about it; I don't think we taped it.

There was a room, maybe thirty by forty in which Benny used to rehearse and next to it was a studio with equipment. It couldn't have been more than twenty by twenty, it had a couch and a console and I used to have to stay in there and monitor the rehearsal; not as an engineer, just to be there. Charlie would come in and go on the couch, racked with TB and high with fever, and I'm sure he wanted to sleep, so he would come in. This was a year before I broke out. I suspect that might have had something to do with it. It affected my
life really after that. It took me out of the rat race, effectively.

If I had had any ambition before that, if I had any proclivity to be ambitious, that just knocked it out of me. It caused me to read a lot and I don't regret it, but it was a lot of years sitting around.
How many years?
Well not consecutively, it went intermittently beginning January, '42 and I was still on the recuperating schedule all through '51; so let's say about ten years.

After that I said the hell with it. When we got Sauter-Finegan, I put a cot on the bus and made sure I got a lot of rest, but I think what saved me there was the laughter. There were a bunch of kooks on that band and it was never boring, I thought it would be awful. In those days we had inherited European chefs and the frozen
food scene had not become epidemic as it is today, so that we ate well. I thought it would be awful, but it wasn't. So I survived, but I think the laughter had the most to do with it.
Especially when you're on the road; that can make a big difference.
I guess you were lucky in the other respect, that Peggy, your wife, was a nurse.

Yes. She'd give me the back of the hand, she wouldn't let you feel sorry for yourself. That kept me, as far as the music business is concerned, probably from making the connections that might have lead to further things. It locked me into a certain area and I never have seen to have gotten out of that.
I got a reputation at that point for being uncommercial, which is the kiss of death. They sent me off to their own special
Siberia through the years, and I never lived that one down either, even though it's no longer true.
Although if you are doing Broadway shows, you can't be totally stigmatized in that regard.
I don't think they see me at all--the people involved in shows don't see me beyond shows. They don't know anything else, they don't know anything else exists.
That's true of a lot of areas of the music business. I have found that everything has their own little cubicle that they're interested in.

Hershey Kaye got me involved in it and the first one turned out to be a hit, Milk and Honey, and he showed me how to do it. So it got the kids through college and it's more or less supplied us with this home, although we still don't own it, it will be couple more years.
You're pretty close though; that's good.
Five years.
You're lucky you got it when you did.
You're not kidding. That's the first time--it also help me pay off the Sauter-Finegan debt. The first couple of years of musicals I didn't retain any of it.
Before that time we couldn't own a house (inaudible). Don't send your kids to Harvard, they can go to NYU, which is fine with me.

Yes he did.
How long were you on that?
They first time was a year. I got seventy five bucks a week for

a year. More important was the gesture, and in those days you could live on it. We had a wonderful house, that one back there; it was when Rockland County was rural and it was a Revolutionary War house; it was charming. It's no longer that way. Fifty seven bucks a month we paid.

This is going somewhere and we're certainly in a period of transition, all the arts. If you look at it one way, you're dead, and it just might be dead too, but on the other hand it may not be. It may be something else is forming, it can't possibly be anything that it was because Pandora's Box has been opened and you can't restuff it. But you somehow have to use what's there and that's the lesson of art anyway, it seems to me. And if living is an art, you better pay heed. We could destroy the whole thing, we have it within our means to destroy it, but that doesn't necessarily follow that we will. But it will never be what it was, so you can shed a tear, if that's the way you feel about it. On the other hand, certain things could get better and the only thing, it seems to me that's stopping it, is the unwillingness to recognize what's there and why it's there. A lot of the evils come
from persisting to pursue the present with the tools of the past. If you use that in art you've got a big problem on your hands.
That's the question of defining the tools of the past. It just isn't always apparent what they were.

I think the hardest thing is to maintain a happy medium. There are some people who just, anything new they can't take, because they're listening totally with the sort of ears the acquired from yesterday. But on the other hand, you have people who embrace anything new just because it's new.
Then there is nothing really new, ever. So what is old, is not old; if there's nothing new then it can never be old.
In each case, they're latching onto something that is a fallacy.

They wandered around a little bit, they weren't that strict about it, but it's what you had to do.
They didn't want Penderecki*?
No.

For Kenton.
It was a different approach in each case, but that was there to be done, I guess, at that time.
I had begun studying with Stefan Wolpe about that same time, late '45, and that opened up a whole world to me, but before that there was always a curiosity of how does

Wolpe was a twelve tone writer, but what a good teacher, what an inspiration- al human being he was.

That's right.

Meanwhile, I was still supposed to be doing things for Ray, but somehow he talked me into that and that let Ray off the hook. I never really went back after that; that was late '48. What happened that time?

It just didn't work out. Then through '49 there wasn't very much there, except getting better. I got a chance to do some things for Decca Records, Gordon Jenkins, toward the end of '49. I thought I was going to get into the Decca crowd at that time, but that didn't work either. Then abruptly in '50 I got sick again.
What kind of things did you do for Decca?

Whatever they needed; vocals mostly. Gordon Jenkins was sort of a house man there. But that collapsed when I got sick and that went for a year, getting over it. Meanwhile, Bill had been sojourning and came back and Johnny Mercer got him to do a musical of his, 'Top Banana' and I was called in to help Bill.
When did you first meet Bill?

He used to live in Tenafly, which is not far from here and he was assigned to the Cap Shanks. I met him early on in the Glenn Miller, but only in passing. I was introduced to him, we talked a bit, but it was never very much. When it came to Shanks, somehow we would spend evenings together. I would go down--he could stay at home and go down to the Army and appear once a month for his check. He had it set up that way.
Cushy deal.

He was the original good soldier schweik (phonetic spelling). Ask Eddie Bert the story, because Eddie was with him through this whole thing. It's very funny; I'm not familiar enough to give the story, but if you ever come out to Bill, get Eddie Bert to tell you.
One story is the lieutenant used to come down and plead, please, come on, show up, so that you can get paid. They were supposed to court martial him or something.
I got Bill then to go to Wolpe. That was after the war though. But it was during these house visits that we used to make just to say hello, really.
I guess it was '47, '48 they went off to Europe.
Wolpe's brother was a consultant, a political consultant, for Time and Life and they helped them get around Paris at the time.

So he came back in '51 and Johnny got him to do the musical--while I was in the hospital in '50 I got a letter from him suggesting we start a band. We can't get along any other way, we might as well prop one another up, which is pretty much what it was.

So he got the musical and I guess it was a disaster because nobody could find anybody, which you just can't do in a show. Just about that time, it began the rage of the secondary Miller bands, everybody was having one.
Ray Anthony, Tex Beneke.
Everybody.

Irv Denken was the trombone player in McKinley's band, got to be at this point a booker with Willard Alexander, although he was still playing trombone, and he picked up on the idea of the two of us going into the thing, his wife jumped on it and we pushed to the point where it was suggested that somebody approach the record companies and see how they would like it.
Both Columbia and RCA did, and for some reason we went with RCA. We wanted one of those composite titles,

like the who or what, just as long as our names weren't involved in it, but we must have spent six months going through a thousand of these things,and some of them were pretty good, but the brass wouldn't accept it. So we wound up being Sauter-Finegan; that was their choice. We got tagged with it, which meant we had to go on the road, which was a disaster.
Originally was it just intended to be a studio--

At that point it was. We just did those dates and it was sold as being better--bigger and better. It wasn't any longer just Miller, it was Goodman plus Miller. That's what they thought they were going to get.
So they didn't think they were going to get anything that was unusal, it was a nostalgia thing.
They were pretty sure that they could sell it by the name,
and if it sounded that way, they figured that one half of the record would sound like Benny and the other half like Miller. And they really didn't want what they got.
How did you manage to get them to record what you wanted to do?
They had to do that because they didn't know beforehand what it was going to be.
They just assumed that because you had written for Goodman and Bill had written for Miller that that's what they were going to get?
Right.

So we came in and did "Doodletown Fifers" and a couple of other things, about four things we had to do the first session and Dave Capp was the A and R man; he was sort of stuck with it at this point. The sales department didn't want any part of that and Dave had to fight for it.

So eventually it was released, and when it was released the disc jockeys picked right up on it and we became one of the proverbial "overnight things", which I wish hadn't happened, because it put us out on the road, where we immediately began to lose money that we didn't have in the first place. Although we waited a year to do it.
There's a quote a few years ago, not very long, Bill did an album for Sonny Stitt--have you heard it, the Sonny Stitt Plays Ellington album?
No, but I remember Bill doing that.
In the notes they talk more about Bill than they do about Stitt, as a matter of fact.
It must be better copy.
There is not much left to say about Stitt I guess. They quote Bill as saying that
That's right. When are you going to play something commercial. The dance thing, Sonny Russo was a funny guy--did you know him?
No. I've heard his playing but that's it.

It was in Kansas, somewhere in Kansas, where this guy comes up and says, when are you going to play something we can dance to and Sonny Russo says, with a horn in his mouth, when are you going to dance to something we can play to.
How did you arrive at the instrumentation for the band?
We were three trumpets, three bones, a tuba, woodwinds,
with all sorts of doubles, and a harp and keyboards, all the keyboards.
Guitar, bass, drums.
And percussionist.

We could have gone into strings and french horns, but that was a little much, we thought. It was gilding a lily, because there was the bother of if not directly, then eventually of transporting those things. I don't know how it would have been if we had gone the other way, but this is the way we went. It might have been costs; costs usually get into those things.
Certainly.
The reason for the combination is that we both couldn't stand the other any longer, because of the block nature of it, where you have to write, it's just stifling.
It's all right if you don't have to do it all the time, so this was the
way we figured we could get out of it, and more than that, we didn't even know if we could get people to play it.

Bill had been in the army with Walter Rosenberger. I remember him calling Rosie down, we had dinner at the Clinton Inn one night discussing how we could do it and it wound up that Rosie and Buster, his partner at the Philharmonic, were the first percussionists (inaudible). They showed us how to do it.

It came really from a desire to--we worked the tunes out and how are we going to do these tunes is really how it was, and any idea that came up required this sort of spacing. We'd sit up in Bill's room where he worked and just talked about it, kicked it back and forth. It was a committee operation. It was a process of elimination really; we needed this to do it.
Bill's lifestyle was totally different from mine. I had the whole regi-

mine of recuperating from TB, which was quite rigid, as far as eating and resting; and Bill never--he was an all nighter and that got to be pretty trying, how to balance this, but somehow we did. I usually gave in on it. Although he tried very hard.

I'm a rotten piano player and he would sit at the piano and we'd kick back and forth how things should go and sometimes I'd have to take it away from him and put it down and say no, that's enough now.
Sometimes I'd force him to write it, because he was a bulldog, he'd hate to let go of his ideas. He wants to pursue it beyond a certain point and sometimes you shouldn't.
As time went on, did you wind up you mostly end up you both each writing your own pieces?
We did that through the first sessions. After that we went out own way.
Both of us were very surprised

when we heard the band, and it was at a good place, on 34th Street, Victor had a union hall next to the hotel, west of Eighth Avenue--I forgot what the name of the place was, but it had a good ring to it. They used to do the NBC symphony broadcast from there too. It was a union hall.
Liederdranz?
No. Liederkranz was 59th Street. This was next to the hotel--New Yorker--but next to it.
Victor, I guess after World War II, did most of their recording there. When they were getting out of closets; then they had just brought in tapes, LP's had just come in which helped us too.
They got a quality on tape that they could never get from those closets, at least it seemed that way. We threw the engineers a curve because it was a big reverberating room and how was he going to
isolate the time. We spent half the time balancing.
I could imagine.
But they did a good job of it, but then we went down a couple of days later and listened to some of these tapes, and my God, it's awful, and we began to think, what would happen now.
I hate bells, no bells; I hate piccolos and as it turned out, a lot of people did, but when they released them they went and a year later they pushed us out on the road.
How did you put the band together, as far as the people you had from the studio days? Were they people that you knew?
Oh, yeah. Some of them we didn't, but most of them we did and most of those we didn't we got through recommendation, as with Rosie and Buster; we knew Don.
Don Lamond?

Yes, and Trigger Alpert (phonetic spelling) had been with Bill Miller's band. Al Klink, Sid Cooper were Miller and Dorsey from Bill's band, and Nick and Joe Ferrante and Bobby Nichols from Dorsey. Nick and Joe Ferrante from McKinley's band. Vern Friley from McKinley's band.
In those times we never used tuba or bass trombone. We had Bill Barber the first time on tuba, because he had been with--we heard him with Gil's thing with Miles.
The Birth of the Cool record.
Was that before us?
Yes, that was '49 and '50.
And you had Moussey Alexander.
That was the road band. We spent weeks with auditions at Carol's studio and we got Harvey Estrom

there and Al Block and Ray Sheiner, Wally King--God bless Wally, Gene Allen; good players. Sonny Russo--we almost didn't get Sonny. Tommy Mitchell wanted to come as a B flat trombonist, wound up being one of the best bass trombonists in the country.
Nick came on the road with us, Bobby did; Joe couldn't--didn't want to, so we had Al Majorca (phonetic spelling) then.
You must have had some fiendish problems especially getting on the road, balancing the woodwinds and all that.

My brother made a monitor system so that we could--he designed the thing and set it up for us. He built it because we had no money and he laid out the money and did it. We could not afford it otherwise. We didn't know how that was going to work either. He did it in such a way that it would just boost that high end, the harp and the celeste; I still have the
downstairs; the glockenspiel, and we didn't buy all this stuff, we rented it all from Carol with the intent to buy; that's what happened.
We had to get a truck to transport it and break in people to handle all this stuff and they didn't always do that well, especially with the sound equipment. They were a little rough with it.
That stuff couldn't take the beatings that it takes now.
But we did it.
One time the truck rolled over in Vermont and the harp went bouncing down a hill. It came to the job that night full of holes; fortunately nobody got hurt, but I'm glad it didn't happen more.
The road is a frightful thing.
Then the other problem that came up was how to write when you're doing one-nighters. That really got me. So we
began to alternate, go home for three or four weeks at a time and come back with a bunch of stuff. That's how we kept it fluid, but not enough still. There was always the pressure there.
I don't know any other way to do it than that.
How did the two of you adjust to finding a band?

Neither one of us had that sort of ego problem; other ego problems, but not that one. As far as we were concerned, the music was what was important and I think the guys respected that too. It took the personality out of it, the music was there; not because of somebody's psychological--
