--psychological problem. Other psychological problems, not that one.
By all accounts, it seems to have been a very happy band.

It was a very musical band, there was a lot of personal respect. I learned an awful lot about people. Looking back, I would hate to say that that never would have happened. It was an experience, a human experience. I hated to be away from the family all that time, as much as you had to be. Both my sons were about ten and eleven; I wanted to be home. The writing time was good.
How long were your tours, as a rule?
Constant; they never stopped. Fifty two weeks a year. It started in May '53 and we stopped in December '55; two and a half
years, a good two and a half years.
Did we say how we stopped it?
You mentioned you had back problems?
Were we on tape when we did that?
I believe so, but let's talk about it a little more. We kind of said it in passing.

Ever since the first time out, we began losing money and it was suggested from the agency, Willard Alexander agency, that we cut down the size of the band and stop playing what we're doing and play dance music. I'm sure that Miller's getting that too, that's the only thing he knows when it comes down to that. But we wouldn't do that, there would be no purpose. I wouldn't do it today; there is no purpose at all in doing it that way. So we said (inaudible) so that we can at least break even, so it doesn't
keep on adding up that way, and that was the end of the band.

One of the things that precipitated it was the government tax, and they were threatening to take it at the gate, which means nobody would get anything, so why get all the way out in the boondocks and have no money and how were we going to get home. That would have been worse than stopping it when we did.
I think it was probably the right thing to do.
That was in '55?
The end of '55, December of '55.
You kept the band going as a recording group for a while.
Yes, as long as the contract lasted. Victor finally decided they didn't want any more of it and stopped it.
That was a few
years later.
Don Costa got the idea we should try something for United Artists, which we hadn't done, but we did it. But that's the last, from then on it was nothing.
If they did sell anything, they didn't let us know. I've never seen a statement from them.
Do you have some favorites among the pieces that you wrote for the band?
A lot of them.

One of them was a piece for flute and piano that they used for a theme song for many years, a program called The Open Mind on NBC. I thought it would have changed my fortune a lot if they gave me credit for some of those things. They used to use Sauter-Finegan things all the time as background music, as dramatic underscoring for dramatic shows, without credit.
I didn't think that was right; I still don't think so.
Did you take them to court over it?
There's nothing you can do about it. If they use a record they're free to do that, so you couldn't. The only way you could do it would be through their good graces, which they did not have.

But it would have changed a lot of things for me had they done that because after Sauter-Finegan, that's really what I wanted to do, but I didn't know how to do it. I didn't arrive at it until Stan did it with Mickey One, but that stopped abruptly, so nothing came out of that. I guess the picture didn't do anything.
You always have to be involved with a hit, and the people want other hits.
One of my
favorite things that I heard from the Sauter-Finegan record is that woodwind thing that you did, "Wild Wings in the Woods."
That's one of mine too. Well done, that thing. There's another one in there I like, "10,000 B.C." That was a tune in a musical I did.
Which is kind of a percussion piece.
Percussion and singer. There were lyrics to that originally, which I couldn't use. It was from a musical called the Reluctant Virgin.
Especially on the one record, Inside Sauter-Finegan, at least half of the things on the record weren't with the full band.
That was asked for by Victor.
One was just Nick
Travis playing, "How About You" with the rhythm section.

That's right. We used to do a lot of things like that on the raod, but this sort of kicked it off. They asked us to make a small band record, because critics loved small bands, in those days particularly. I think the critics pushed this way and that's one of the reasons for the rise of rock; that's one reason, there are others. They didn't like the big bands; they still don't. They'd been castigated and Harvey Estern (phonetic spelling) had use of the library for the rehearsal band at the YMHA, and the bigness of the band there (inaudible). It might be too much for some people, but anyway, we did it because RCA asked us to, and the other part of it was that on the road after playing all night, the smallness is welcomed. We used to feel a sense of relief from
doing that. Another one I like in there was "Eddie and the Witch Doctor". I don't know where these names came about.
That was percussion; that was Moussey's piece.
The notes for all of those records, you and Bill, I guess wrote them, and they were very funny with a very dry sense of humor.
I'm glad you got that. One of the things I tried to get into those notes, is the respect of the people.
Oh, very definitely.
I wanted it that way; I hope that came across.
Where did you get the singers that you had?
Sally came--
Sally Sweetland.

She was in Ray Charles--one of the Ray Charles Singers and just got with the band, I guess. We needed somebody and I asked Sally to come and she did.

And Andy Roberts was doing a TV show on WPIX, I think, with Mundy (phonetic spelling) and Mundy said come over and hear the guy and we went over and talked to him and he would come too.

Andy for years has been a sportscaster, a weatherman, in Norfolk, Virginia. He's a wonderful guy and a good singer too. I don't think we did justice to him on the records; it's too bad, but then with the band, his sort of singing went off with the rock scene too.
Where is he now?
He's a sportscaster-weatherman--
Oh, that's where
Yes; Norfolk, Virginia. He's been there for years.

Sally had been married to an opera singer who was drafted at the wrong moment and it wrecked his career, because he had been at the Met and when he came back they no longer--he was too old for it or something.

He began teaching and when Sally left the band that's what they did; they went to the coast. I don't know where he comes from, and they set up a studio, which they still run. I guess it's in North Hollywood. She's a vocal coach and he is too.
I take it your relations with Bill were, on the whole, pretty good.
I always respected his talent. Bill has, like everybody, problems, but if you can--I don't think I

could work as closely with anybody again, because his work habits and mine are just too different, but that was really the only problem. Intellectually we got along very well; a great respect for his talent, which most people do, I'm not alone in that.
Certainly not.
I think probably one of the--a real genius is in there crying to come out; I've always felt that. He should be (inaudible) and not some of the people who are, because they can't cut it.

I think I mentioned this to you--Don Sebesky wrote an arranging book called, The Contemporary Arranger, a few years ago, and he spent a good amount of space just talking about your band and talking about the impact that it had on studio recordings, and he said something to the effect that if you can find any of the Sauter-Finegan records, buy them, because they sound as fresh now as
That's the truth. You know why I think so?
Why?

Because they were both written and played with the idea of bringing out a life thing. I think it's that life that sticks with us. It's just something that has to be, at that time. It can sound pretty dull if it's not played right, but it was played very well. It took a lot of effort and a lot of time to do it that way though, you don't walk in and walk out of the studio in three or four hours.
When you had a road band, did you have a band turnover or did guys stay with you for quite a while?
They stayed as long as they wanted to. One time everybody left at once, and then we began having troubles--not real troubles, because somehow it
always shaped up again, but it began lacking the security that it had. Really, what both Bill and I wanted was an Ellington-type thing.
Where you're writing for specific people?
Yes.

It was unfortunate that our names were there, because it gave the impression that we were entrepreneurs who were using people for our personal gain, which was not so. We both wanted to make it some sort of cooperative thing without ever really knowing how to do it and it would be unfair to do that when things weren't going too well. When things are bad, you make it cooperative and as soon as it gets good, you forget about it.
We don't know; it's all academic now anyhow, how that would have turned out.
Most of them got off the road because of family problems; they had to.
That was true of Moussey and Nick and I kept replacing them. Harvey Estrom had to go too.
Joe Venudo became kind of a star in the band, didn't he? He was featured on a lot of different percussion.
Yes, he was a very electric sort of person. I guess he did very well as a percussionist after that.
As a studio musician; yeah.

He's in Reno now. We had Sperry Karas (phonetic spelling), who got drafted into the Seventh Army Symphony, was was instrumental in setting up that German episode. That was an experience, a unique one, but that didn't last very long though.
How did that come about? That was around '55 or something?
We had gotten off
the road at the end of '55 and the only-- now I had two kids ready to go to school, to higher education, and I had no means of putting them there.

A whole year I couldn't get any work in the studios in New York and the only income was an occasional weekend, which Wil- lard was forcing us to do, because we said we're not going out until--don't make us go out--so we went out with pick up bands, which was terrible.
You mean you'd go out to some town and get a bunch of locals?
Yes.
That must have been a disaster.
It was.

They rought them here because they weren't eating over there.

Yes. You were there for how long?
Twenty months or something like that. It was a three year contract.
Other than those hassles, how as living over there?
Good. I liked the people very much, but it just didn't work out properly. The living was great. I think I'll take a run
over there this autumn if I get a chance. I like to, to say hello to everybody.
I came back here and there was nothing. Ray Sheiner, the oboist, got me onto a couple of commercials, but I couldn't live on what I was getting.
Hershey Kay latched onto a musical and I started doing that. So then we began eating a little regularly and the kids went to school and we got all that taken care of.
That's about where it's been ever since.

I went to the coast in '71 to do 1776 and ran into the chap I was talking about earlier at MCA. None of them came off as
musical, but he drifted to the coast and became a producer, director out there, and it was his show, it had to be "Night Gallery", so I did that and that was good.

I did a season and a half, until it went off the air.
That was the early seventies, or something like that?
I started the middle of '71 and it took us through '72 when I stopped.

Every once in a while he calls me out to do something, but that's the only guy I know. I liked that but I didn't feel it was strong enough to move out to the coast and take my chances, because there's no reason to think that I would be any more commercially viable than I was here.

They know where to find you.
I don't even think they think, but I have also learned that when I go around looking for things, nothing happens. You like to do that? That's nice, but they never call.

It was so bad to the point, I think it gave me a heart attack at one point, and I have stopped thinking about it.

In '66, after not working for about three years. Up until then I could always get away with it, thinking there would be a tomorrow; at one point I realized there won't be a tomorrow, and I think that's what kicked it off.

He didn't like the arbitrary of using that aspect, say on Beethoven, where you sit at the master's seat with great reverence and play each phrase of each situation that has been passed down by rote through the years--
As if it were engraved in stone.

Yeah. And missing the real point of the thing possibly in the process, so that all you're doing is imitating--or you're following the rules set down by almost everyone else than Beethoven, something else of the period that Beethoven wrote it, the cultural feel of that period. Subsequent cultures don't really respond to that.

His music, as played by the Julliard quartet, and especially the (inaudible) quartet, it roared--Beethoven roared. Such a magnificent great man. (Inaudible). If you can bring a sense of enduring or substance to a contemporary piece (inaudible).
Assuming that that attitude is present, is it possible
Why not?
I think what's important is to get the essence of what that was and to build on it and not to imitate it, to make it come alive. In other words, it has to live; if it doesn't live it's nothing.
There's an ironic little twist there, on that particular piece. I don't know if you heard a later recording that Duke did of that in 1956.
He had a different band and he redid some of those pieces. He played "Koko" again and it was--
Totally different.
--not very good.
It didn't swing very well.
They had an off day.
Yeah, that may have been the only thing that went wrong, is that they had an off day.
Who knows about the quality of the A & R man at that time?
Yeah. But even when the guy who wrote the piece tries to do it over again, it may not work for various reasons.

No two performers are alike; thank God. There is no such thing as a definitive performer, there is only one that can isolate it per recording, or one that is allowed to grow. Before recording all we had was memory. We're talking about the way people listened in those days. You'd be exposed, maybe work alongside someone or work for someone who had a great influence on your thinking after that, but you went on with the memory of all this and built on it. It wasn't as though you could ever turn the tape on it and listen to it happen again, because what happened on that
tape was something of the moment; it had no real validity after that. You can use it just as you use a photograph. It's okay, but don't misrepresent with it.
You mentioned how people listen to music; how did people listen to Sauter-Finegan in 1954, say if you were on a typical one nighter?

Well, I think you have to realize that there were no groups around touring like that. The people who did come were mostly expecting to dance. It was sold as a dance band, which was unfortunate. We spent most of our time trying to satisfy them but never really doing it.
Did you pull out something like "Wild Wings of the Woods" once in a while?
Once in a while we did and I remember being in Iowa before that Lieberman concert in '54--we were at
practice or something--and towards the end of the evening we dragged that thing out and played our part and the people really didn't know what was going on. But some of them kind of liked it.
I'm sure that it must have been a totally different experience for most of them.
I think they were bewildered, a lot of them. Those who knew some of the records, did like it. They never did break down the gates to get in; that's for sure.
Which is the problem you had all along.
I want to ask you about a statement you made to me a few days ago. You said something to the effect that you really felt that you hadn't been part of the "jazz scene"--
I still feel like that.
Do you think that's true throughout your career or--
Yes. I always felt like that.
Even when you were writing for Norvo or Goodman?
Yes.
Or writing for jazz musicians? Why do you feel like that?
Why?
Yes.
I don't know, maybe because I was always made to feel that the written note was somehow not desirable.
A necessary evil?
Yes. We are always writing pretty much (inaudible). I got around that by studying alot and by taking lessons. I was just as baffled by people like Bartok and Stravinsky; how did they do it? How
can it be that someone could be that good? I felt that way about performing jazz musicians too.
Don't you think the problem you describe is one that any arranger who is a composer and/or arranger who has worked in the jazz field?

I don't know. I can't know what they really feel. You know, there is one thing that I did fail to mention and I think I should, since this is a historical thing, around 1959 or so, when I should really have gone and taken a fly on the west coast on film, there came a letter from California Tax Department to the effect that if either of these two guys show up in California and we know about it, the first thing we'll do is put them in San Quentin.
What?
Yes. And I think that letter might still be with (inaudible).
I told him to keep it; whether he did or not I don't know. That kept me from going there.
Why, between Uncle Sam and the California State Government, why did they take such an aggressive and hostile tact towards you and Bill?
Because I think it was assumed we were quite successful, for one thing--
(Side B of Tape 5 ends at this point. Transcript will continue with Tape 6.)
(Tape 6 begins at this point.)
The other thing is that it was a typical, squareish reaction to anyone who is involved in art, especially in show business; they assumed they're essentially irresponsible brats.
You said you eventually paid off all of those debts; right?
Yes, but it took a long time.
I could imagine. Did the record company, RCA specifically, did they finance the tours you did at all?
No, all they did was advance money to record, but we still haven't, and never will, get any money from those records.
You know, of course, that it's much more common now for a record company to finance a tour by a
performing group, or an appearance in a club or on television, or whatever.
I know that they do it, but they only do it under duress. They never really want to, they're forced to do it, and obviously they weren't in those days.
The other thing I wanted was to do all original things and that was not acceptable either by the record company.
(Inaudible)
Here's a conjectual question.
Do you think that if you had started Sauter-Finegan say twenty five years after you did, the climate today would be better for acceptance of the band?
I doubt it, because it was very much a part of its time, it wasn't ahead of its time or behind it; it was right then. It was a result of my reaction and Bill's reaction and all the

people in the band to the life around them. It grew out of that period, and you can reconstruct that period to a point, but you can never do the whole thing, you can never go the whole way. It becomes a facsimile somehow.
Would you still be interested in writing for that type of instrumentation?
Not really; no.
You had your fill of it?

Yes. You have to have stimulus, you have to follow a need too, and that was the need at that time. It had something to do with my age too and my position in life, what was happening to me. None of that exists any longer. I don't have the energy I had then, although I didn't have that much energy then either.
You were getting
over a long bout with TB.
There was a period between then when I had lots of energy. I don't worry about that anymore.
Have you ever talked--I'm sure you talked with Bill somewhere at different points, about his feelings about the experience you had together.
Oh, sure.
What did he have to say?
Bill feels it probably more deeply than I do (inaudible).

As I think I mentioned before, Don Sebesky seems to think that you were ahead of your time as far as some of the concepts you introduced and the whole new dimension that you got, indirectly, in the studio recording.
We couldn't be, because they grew they grew up, really, out of frustration of that time, the things
that bugged Bill and bugged me that we didn't want to be involved in. We were forced to do these things.
You just didn't want to write for five saxes.
That's one of them.
Or a block brass section
We wanted our music to say something that had an emotional spray, if you like--how do you describe it--there are no words to describe--you can say moved if you like.

Music expresses a whole gamut of a person's emotional capability; it can be deep, it can be shallow, it can be everything, and that's the relationship, the drama, the fact that it can do this. Also in poetry, the relationship to poetry, it loses the time element, the lyrics (inaudible).
Didn't we talk about this before?
Not really.

I seem to remember saying--mentioning that lyrics are an edge of poetry, not of music and a popular misconception is that lyrics are music; they're not, they're part of poetry. Music is an art of putting sound and rhythm together, time and space. (inaudible)
I'd like to have my hearing in twenty five years.
(Inaudible)

Have you heard the work of any composers and arrangers say in the jazz or popular music field since you had Sauter-Finegan, where you thought they may have picked up on some of the concepts that you and Bill had?
I never thought of it that way. I'm always looking for someone to come and do what we tried to do, and I haven't heard anybody do that yet.
(Inaudible)
Philosophy, a record company are all factors.
(Inaudible).
What's your philosophy for writing on strings?
No different than writing for anything else, except--no, no except. Strings have a quality that have to be strings (inaudible).
The individual quality?

Yeah. (inaudible) The violin really depends on the player, as does everything else. The violin itself does nothing, it's a means to produce a sound and you have physical limitations to produce that sound, and you have to think of that, but not too much. (Inaudible). You shouldn't do certain things

that are obviously--that can be done the same thing in a simpler fashion--you can always try to do that, but I don't think that you need to be an accomplished violinist to do these things. You need to have the ability to think musically, and I think the violinist will respect what you've done (inaudible).

That's why almost all composers that I know, have always consulted whoever they're writing the piece for before they eventually let the publishing be done. Sometimes they'll redraft it three or four times because of things like that.

You must think that there is a guy behind every horn, a human being who has to eat, he has to take air, he has to move his fingers, purse his lips however. Different instruments speak in a different fashion; you have to know that.
Did you have this kind of interplay with the concert-
No.
Who was the concertmaster on that? They don't give credit.
They don't?
Not on the re-issue of Focus; maybe on the original record they did.
That was the Beaux Arts String Quartet, the guy's name was--later he got into the Composers String Quartet--Jerry--I hope he doesn't hear this tape--I'll get it.

There was nothing really that difficult on that. I didn't want to use a rhythm section; that was one of the things I knew I didn't want to use, because I don't like the brittle sound of a rhythm section playing (inaudible).
You can set up a feeling and it is immediately wiped out, and if that's
what you want to do, great, but I didn't want that.

There's a self conscious pacing that jazz has or jazz players have when they go into their "schtick" that doesn't fit with the symphonic jazz concept. I never heard anything that worked along those lines, nothing. So I never really tried it, I never wanted to try it.
We did the (inaudible).

I heard an interesting story about Wes Montgomery. When Wes made his recordings in the sixties with Don Sebesky, it got to a point that Wes-- apparentlyonce they got him in the studio they tried to do the recording there with string players and woodwind players, and he was just so intimidated by the whole process they eventually just had him come in with the rhythm section and laid down his tracks, and then Sebesky would write the padding around it.
(Inaudible)
No, it couldn't be if they were writing around.
Unless what they did was Sebesky took over (inaudible).
I guess there's more than one side to a problem like that.
Maybe he was reacting the same way I was reacting. I know that happened with Stan-- although he doesn't admit it--up in Tanglewood. He asked me to write a piece for him--did we discuss this?
Not in detail, no.
There's this huge hall and you get overwhelmed by this and I wrote a (inaudible). Everything fell down and he was reading off the floor at one point.
In that case, did they make--this was for the Boston Pops;
Yes.
Did they make you a trap drummer in that instance; when the do their "jazz" thing they usually have somebody playing a set.
No. Manny Albam did the "Girl From Ipanema" with a trap set, and Alec Wilder had a piece--
Oh, Alec did something for him?
Yes.
"The Bad and the Beautiful" has simulated jazz.
We always felt that the jazz thing (inaudible). In my early years, I used to not want to mix it (inaudible). I don't think any of us would do it now or even attempt it.
What do you think of a piece like Milhaud's Creation du Monde?
I think they call it jazz; I don't think it is.
I don't think so either, but it incorporates certain influences say that Milhaud heard when he was in this country.
Do you think things like that can work?
Yes, because he breathed and absorded it and made it part of himself. (inaudible).
Stravinsky too--
Say Ebony Concerto.
Well you could, but you could also be l'Histoire du Soldat or Ragtime*(inaudible), which are vintage Stravinsky. (Inaudible)
Any good composer, they're all working with twelve tones, I guess when you get right down to it.
The tones are the
* Franklin Society, Franklin Mint.

least of it. Tones are part of the tools you use, but so much has been made of that, it seems to me. An awful lot of books have come out through the years and they all say the same thing, and most of them say nothing. They all seem to be involved in proving what is easily proven. One of the easiest things to get onto is notes. But you try to use any of that stuff and it's very difficult, it doesn't work. There's something we're all groping for and nobody achieves.
What's that something?
I don't know.
(Inaudible).
One thing I didn't ask you, do you write at the piano or away from it?
Mostly at it. I try away, but I never--piano is a crutch for me. That comes from being a trumpet
I've known guys who sit in the back of a bus and write a piece and I marvel at that, but I can't do it.

Don't be in any more awe of that than you should be of people (inaudible). It's something that some people have and some very often have been trained. It doesn't mean that you don't write better pieces; not at all. Sometimes it's the convenience that's taken for granted, they don't work hard enough. Some people should work hard (inaudible). It comes too easy for them.
(Inaudible)
Maybe they'll learn a little bit about themselves in the process.
Certainly Stravinsky and Bartok and you name them, have done this for me and I don't know any of
them. What has been important is what their music has done to me. To me; not for me.

By the way, we probably should get on tape, if you wish, what you mentioned about George Simon calling you this morning and saying they are interested in putting out a recording of some of the Sauter-Finegan material. Do you want to describe that?
More than that I don't know. He simply informed me of what is happening, he's putting the thing together for the Franklin Society. Beyond that I really don't know.
Is there any kind of a chance that you know of that more of that material would be put out, and how would you like to see it reissued? Do you have any ideas about that?
At this point I don't care. If I have any concern (inaudible).

Other than bread and butter I don't care about it. If it provides me with shelter and food and clothing, and increasingly, drugs for health reasons, because I'm getting older; if I don't have to go begging for that sort of thing that's fine. If that could in any way provide me with the necessities, then it's important to me; otherwise, it's not.
You're not particularly interested in what that music is as a legacy?
I never thought in terms of after death. It's a life thing to me. If I die, it's all gone, that's when it all stops.
I get the impression that you're interested primarily in new talent.
In talent, period. I don't know if new has to be there, probably yes. It doesn't mean that I'm looking
That's a viewpoint that many other composers have had, and I think it's a perfectly legitimate one.
It has to be for me.
There weren't too many Charles (inaudible) who would pack it in a barn.
(Inaudible).
Well, as you said earlier, you envision specific people that you're writing for. He obviously couldn't.
That's the way he was brought up though. He did grow up on the other side of the tracks, musically. (Inaudible).
I'm not sure I follow that last remark entirely. Could you explain a little more?
Well I feel I've been on the outside of classical music too,
I've never been on the inside of that. Maybe partly because I've never been a performer (inaudible).
Let's see, what other things do we have to discuss?
I'm sure there are other things, but what?
I'm wracking my brain.
You'll come up with something in a couple of days.
Perhaps. I always do.
If you think of something we could have another session. At the moment I can't think of anything.
At the moment I feel we've done a pretty thorough job.
There's no point in being redundant about it.
In which case, let's sign off for now.
(End of interview.)
